entries.title: Norway's PM: Zelenskyy's plane almost hit by drone
entries.summary: A drone nearly struck a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo, according to Norway's prime minister. However, a Ukrainian source said the threat may have been overstated.
entries.content:
Norway

Norway's PM: Zelenskyy's plane almost hit by drone

September 9, 2026

A drone nearly struck a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo, according to Norway's prime minister. However, a Ukrainian source said the threat may have been overstated.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said on Wednesday that a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo for the funeral of Norway's recently deceased King Harald V was almost hit by a drone.

"His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in," Store told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK, adding that Zelenskyy had left Norway for Canada, where he would meet with leaders in Ottawa.

Store provided no further details about the incident, which reportedly happened on Tuesday, as Zelenskyy was en route from Moldova to Norway.

The Ukrainian president arrived in Oslo on Tuesday evening. In the Norwegian capital, he held talks with Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide and Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg regarding military aid, including air-defense support, as well as civilian assistance.

On Wednesday, Zelenskyy then joined other foreign dignitaries at the funeral of King Harald.

Russian drone in Moldova

Meanwhile, neither Ukrainian authorities nor Zelenskyy himself have commented on the drone incident.

A source in the Ukrainian presidency provided a more nuanced account of the situation to AFP: "There was an alert in Moldova when a Russian drone entered Moldovan and Romanian airspace."

The claim that Zelenskyy was at risk was described as "exaggerated" by the source.

According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) — a US think tank — a Russian drone flew in Moldovan and Romanian airspace for about an hour on Tuesday.

The ISW said the defense ministries of Moldova and Romania both reported that a Shahed drone entered Moldovan airspace from Ukraine, flew over Romania, and then returned to Moldova, where it crashed.

However, it is unclear whether this was the same drone mentioned by Store.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: China: English to be removed as a graded core subject?
entries.summary: A university professor is calling for English to no longer be taught as a graded core subject in Chinese schools. Opponents argue that, in a globalized world, knowing English is beneficial for the country and career.
entries.content:
September 9, 2026

A university professor is calling for English to no longer be taught as a graded core subject in Chinese schools. Opponents argue that, in a globalized world, knowing English is beneficial for the country and career.

From business and academia to social media and entertainment — English is considered the dominant global language. One in five people on Earth actively uses this lingua franca. In China, a mathematics professor specializing in vector algebra is now challenging this dominance in no uncertain terms. Tang Jiafeng believes that English should be abolished as a core subject in elementary schools, secondary schools and universities.

Tang is convinced that no other country in the world has placed as much importance on English as China has.

"Our children desperately begin learning English even before they have properly mastered their native language. Yet we are a civilization that dates back thousands of years. English is just a tool. It's enough to be able to use it. The tradition of revering and emulating Western cultures must come to an end," Tang says in social media.

English as a required subject starting in third grade

English is considered difficult in China, since the Chinese language does not use an alphabetic script. It is a required subject starting in third grade. It is graded on par with Chinese and mathematics on the entrance exam for secondary schools, the central exam after 9th grade, and the high school graduation exam. A maximum of 150 points can be earned on the latter.

"How many resources and how much time do our children, parents and schools invest in a subject that is completely irrelevant to the majority of people in their future professional lives?" the mathematician asks, explaining his position.

He became well-known because many of his students achieved full scores on state math exams; in the class of 2011, six students from a single class did so.

Why English? 'AI translates'

Tang's opinion spread quickly online.

"Why cram for English when artificial intelligence can translate everything in seconds?" comments a user from Beijing.

Another suggestion from the southern province of Guangdong is to at least adjust the scoring — for example, to 120 points instead of 150 on the high school graduation exam.

Many parents invest in private tutoring that focuses specifically on exam questions. In addition, all bachelor's students must pass the English exam before being admitted to master's programs. Tang suspects that this could cause many young talents in the natural sciences to fail, even though they have great potential to become top researchers.

No English proficiency, no competitiveness

There is no question that English is also important for STEM subjects. Research on future-oriented topics is typically published in English. There are fears circulating online that cutting back on English instruction could lead to a decline in China's competitiveness. A prominent advocate for English as a required subject is Hu Xijin, former editor-in-chief of the state-run "Global Times," who has previously drawn attention primarily for his nationalistic statements.

Hu emphasizes that foreign language skills are of great importance for every global citizen, "because we live primarily in the present," alluding to a debate over the ungraded history exam. "This present is shaped by globalization. China's opening up is not only state policy but also expands people's scope of action as well as the range of their diverse material and immaterial interests in life."

Hu went on to say that connections to the outside world should not, therefore, be compared to intellectual ties to ancient history.

"Forcibly pitting them against each other — by asking whether foreign languages or traditional Chinese culture are more important — runs the risk of setting the wrong priorities and unnecessarily politicizing public discussions."

For him, an open engagement with the outside world is the top priority. English as a core subject also promotes equal opportunity, he noted, as it gives children in rural areas access to this important foreign language and thus to the world.

Little interest in language studies

Even Chinese universities specializing in foreign languages are feeling the pressure to adjust their educational goals and prepare incoming freshmen for future job markets. For example, fewer and fewer high school graduates are interested in German language studies, explains a university professor from Beijing who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity.

The new curriculum at Beijing Foreign Studies University has adopted a "foreign language plus major" model: English combined with law, information technology, or economics.

Similar cultural struggles already took place during the Self-Strengthening Movement in the late 19th century under the Qing Dynasty.

"Learn the superior skills from abroad so that you can later conquer the outside world," said Wei Yuan, a court scholar at the time.

Learning from abroad simply works better in the language used there. Even though it may be becoming apparent that, in some areas, other countries are more interested in learning from China— as is already the case today, for example in battery technology for the automotive industry, and humanoid robotics.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Ceuta: EU grants Spain €115 million in emergency aid
entries.summary: The EU has said the funds will go toward bolstering border security and returning migrants to Morocco. The move comes in the wake of a crisis that saw more than 70,000 migrants overwhelm the Spanish exclave in July.

entries.title: Germany's connection to the September 11, 2001 attacks
entries.summary: The 9/11 attacks were partly planned in Hamburg, via the so-called Hamburg cell, whose members played key roles in the plot. A look back at a day that shook up Germany’s approach to national security.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany's connection to the September 11, 2001 attacks

September 9, 2026

The 9/11 attacks were partly planned in Hamburg, via the so-called Hamburg cell, whose members played key roles in the plot. A look back at a day that shook up Germany’s approach to national security.

"This day has changed the world," German President Johannes Rau said. He had watched in shock as the burning Twin Towers of the World Trade Center collapsed in New York.

Nearly 3,000 people were killed on September 11, 2001, when Islamist terrorists hijacked four passenger planes and turned them into deadly weapons.

Eleven Germans among the victims

Germany’s head of state struggled to find the right words: "We do not know what political or social consequences what happened today will have — what we have watched unfold on our television screens in shock, barely able to comprehend or even reflect on it."

It soon emerged that the victims include people from 92 countries, among them 11 Germans.

The following day, a rapidly spreading rumor was confirmed: Three of the four suspected hijackers had recently lived in Hamburg. The Islamist terrorists were thought to have been led by Egyptian-born Mohammed Atta, who had come to the northern German city in the early 1990s to study.

Mohammed Atta becomes radicalized at a mosque

At some point, the young man became radicalized, particularly at Hamburg's Al-Quds Mosque, which was later closed by German security authorities. He spent the final three years of his life in an apartment shared with two other suspected attackers in the Harburg district.

The so-called Hamburg terrorist cell was believed to have included six men, among them Moroccan national Mounir al-Motassadeq. He was charged as an accomplice in the world's first trial related to the September 11, 2001, attacks. In 2003, the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court sentenced him to the maximum 15-year prison term for aiding and abetting thousands of murders and for membership in a terrorist organization.

A man from Bremen at Guantanamo

After serving his sentence, al-Motassadeq was deported to his native Morocco. Another suspected attacker from the circle around pilot Mohammed Atta was Ramzi Binalshibh, who was born in Yemen and had been held without trial at the US detention facility at Guantanamo Bay since 2006.

The United States detained hundreds of suspects at the prison, which human rights groups and international bodies have described as contrary to international law. Among them was Murat Kurnaz, who was born in Bremen. He was released in August 2006 after nearly five years without evidence establishing his involvement in the terrorist attacks.

Kurnaz later recounted his experience in a book that was adapted into a film in 2013.

Frank-Walter Steinmeier before investigative committee

Meanwhile, investigative committees in the German Bundestag sought to determine why Kurnaz and other suspects had wrongly come under the scrutiny of American and German intelligence agencies. Among those called to testify was then-Foreign Minister and current German PresidentFrank-Walter Steinmeier.

At the center of the inquiry was the question of why German security authorities rejected the possible return in 2002 of the German-born detainee, who held a Turkish passport.

"No one doubts, and neither do I, that Mr. Kurnaz suffered terribly in Guantanamo," Steinmeier said. "That is why we also sought to ensure that he was treated in accordance with the rule of law. But at the same time, please understand that we were also obliged to ensure security in our own country."

Gerhard Schröder voiced 'unconditional solidarity'

The Kurnaz case illustrated the pressure on German policymakers in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks in the US. Chancellor Gerhard Schröder addressed parliament the following day. 

"Yesterday, September 11, 2001, will go down in history as a dark day for all of us," the Social Democrat said.

He said he had expressed to the American president the deeply felt condolences of the entire German people.

"I also assured him of Germany's unconditional — I emphasize: unconditional — solidarity," Schröder said.

Germany, he added, would offer the US any assistance they requested, "of course, also by identifying and pursuing those responsible for and behind these despicable attacks."

Bundestag passes anti-terror laws

Schröder's remarks set the tone and opened the door for a series of tougher laws. Just weeks after the attacks, the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens unveiled its first so-called security package, involving more funding, more personnel as well as greater powers for police and intelligence agencies.

Religious organizations that had previously been granted special protection could now be banned like other associations if their activities were directed against the Basic Law, Germany's constitutional order based on freedom and democracy, or if they pursued other criminal aims. Less than four months after the terrorist attacks in the US, Germany's Anti-Terrorism Act took effect.

Intelligence agencies were given access to personal data held by banks, airlines and telecommunications companies. Immigration laws were tightened.

Through data-mining searches, in which large amounts of data were cross-checked without any specific suspicion, authorities sought to identify so-called sleeper agents — people like Mohammed Atta from the Hamburg terrorist cell, who had not been identified by security agencies in time.

The Federal Constitutional Court brought an end to the legally questionable practice. Such searches were permissible only when there was a specific threat, the court said in a 2006 ruling. Seven years later, Germany's highest court also ruled that parts of the country's anti-terrorism database were unconstitutional.

Germany signs up for the war in Afghanistan

The Islamist terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, also had far-reaching and lasting military consequences. The US launched attacks on the Taliban in Afghanistan as early as October 2001. The Taliban had refused to hand over Osama bin Laden, the head of the al-Qaeda terrorist network and suspected mastermind of the attacks.

Germany joined the US-led war in December 2001. The conflict lasted 20 years and ended in August 2021 with the Taliban's return to power. Around 3,600 soldiers from the international forces were killed, including 59 members of Germany's Bundeswehr. Three German police officers also died.

The words spoken by German President Johannes Rau on Sept. 11, 2001, in the aftermath of the Islamist terrorist attacks in the US, still resonate today: "This day has changed the world."

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Serbia, the conflicted EU candidate
entries.summary: On paper, Belgrade has pursued EU membership for years. But accession has long been stalled. The hero's farewell given to war criminal Mladic exposed just how far Serbia has alienated itself from Europe.
entries.content:
Europe

Serbia, the conflicted EU candidate

September 9, 2026

On paper, Belgrade has pursued EU membership for years. But accession has long been stalled. The hero's farewell given to war criminal Mladic exposed just how far Serbia has alienated itself from Europe.

The state-supported funeral of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade this week has raised a pressing question in Brussels: Can a country seek EU membership while giving a hero's farewell to a convicted war criminal? For many, the event has shown that Serbia's accession process has not merely stalled. It has largely lost its political drive.

"For too long, the EU has kept treating Serbia as a normal candidate country," Engjellushe Morina of the European Council on Foreign Relations told DW, despite Belgrade's continued backsliding on democracy and the rule of law.

Naim Leo Besiri of Serbia's Institute for European Affairs adds: "The ruling majority in Serbia has not performed anything that was promised on the reform agenda during the last five years."

A candidate moving away from Europe

Both experts point out that Belgrade has refused to join EU sanctions against Russia. Democratic standards have deteriorated under nationalist President Aleksandar Vucic, while relations with Kosovo remain tense.

Despite having been sentenced to life imprisonment by a UN court for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, Ratko Mladic was buried in Belgrade on Monday with military honors and the participation of government representatives. President Vucic stayed away, but facilitated and defended the public mourning.

Brussels reacted unusually strongly. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the images shocking. European Council President Antonio Costa condemned the glorification of war criminals. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a visit to Serbia.

Has the EU been too lenient?

But both Morina and Besiri say that this is not enough. They believe Vucic has been given too much room to maneuver for too long. In their perception, he has been treated as an indispensable partner who could secure stability in the Western Balkans and keep Serbia anchored to the West, despite disregarding basic European values.

Besiri says Serbian civil society had warned Brussels for years about attacks on media freedom, the rule of law and democratic institutions. But, he adds, the EU largely turned a blind eye.

Economic relations demonstrate the strong ties between the EU and Serbia. The bloc is Serbia's largest trading partner, investor and financial donor. Politically, however, Serbia has developed a close partnership with Moscow.

A common argument for continuing relations with Serbia is therefore based on the concern that greater pressure could push the country further towards Russia or China.

Strong economic ties, close relations with Moscow

Morina accepts that isolating Serbia would be dangerous, but sees other options between accommodation and abandoning relations altogether. The EU should remain engaged with Serbian society while forcing Vucic to make clear political choices, she argues.

Besiri says Russia and China could never replace the European market. In his view, Vucic uses both countries as a threat to discourage Brussels from taking firmer action.

Both researchers see strategies behind the current approach: Vucic benefits from cooperation without implementing the necessary reforms. Brussels, meanwhile, can continue to claim that Serbia remains tied to Europe.

The limits of financial pressure

The EU has not remained entirely inactive. It has started applying financial pressure. Further payments under the Growth Plan for the Western Balkans have been withheld because of concerns about judicial independence.

Besiri doubts that this will change Vucic's calculations. Broad funding cuts could hurt the population more than the political elite, he argues. Instead, he advocates targeted measures against those responsible for the country's democratic decline and the misuse of its institutions.

Could the election bring change?

The early parliamentary election on October 25 could put Vucic's model to the test. After 12 years as president, he now wants to remain Serbia's dominant political figure by becoming the next prime minister.

Besiri says that the political opposition in Serbia remains fragile and that "it is extremely difficult to win democratically in undemocratic elections."

Neither expert expects one election to repair Serbia's institutions or fundamentally change its relationship with the EU.

Reconciliation remains a distant prospect

Reconciliation in the region appears even more distant. According to Besiri, Serbia would first have to acknowledge its role in the wars of the 1990s and accept established facts about the crimes committed. Instead, narratives portraying Serbs exclusively as victims remain deeply embedded in Serbian politics, education and the media.

"What has been happening recently is basically the reverse of everything that has been built for so many years," Morina underlines.

Mladic's funeral did not cause this development, she adds. It simply revealed once again how far Serbia currently remains from both regional reconciliation and EU membership.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: Switzerland: Two killed in power plant explosion
entries.summary: A fire and subsequent explosion have killed two workers at a Swiss hydroelectric power plant. Authorities say the facility suffered major damage in the incident.
entries.content:
Europe

Switzerland: Two killed in power plant explosion

September 9, 2026

A fire and subsequent explosion have killed two workers at a Swiss hydroelectric power plant. Authorities say the facility suffered major damage in the incident.

Two workers were killed in an explosion at a hydroelectric power plant in the village of Piotta in southern Switzerland on Wednesday, according to local authorities.

Police say a fire was reported at the Ritom Hydroelectric Station in the canton of Ticino around 9:30 a.m. (0730 GMT). The blaze trapped two workers inside.

Shortly thereafter, an explosion rocked the plant, severely damaging the building and gravely injuring the men, both of whom died from their injuries shortly thereafter.

Authorities say one of the men was a a 55-year-old Swiss citizen, the other has yet to be identified.

State prosecutors have launched an investigation into the cause of the deadly incident.

The facility, which is owned by Swiss rail carrier SBB, is currently undergoing renovations as part of a plan to reconfigure the 100-year-old site.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Iran tightens social control with crackdown on cafes
entries.summary: Authorities are keeping a close eye on cafes, fearing they could play a role in fostering anti-government sentiment.
entries.content:
Asia

Iran tightens social control with crackdown on cafes

September 9, 2026

Authorities are keeping a close eye on cafes, fearing they could play a role in fostering anti-government sentiment.

Iranian authorities have launched a clampdown on cafes in the capital, Tehran, in recent months, suspecting them of fostering anti-government sentiment and facilitating protests.  

According to the human rights organization HRANA, at least seven cafes and restaurants were shut down on July 19 alone for allegedly failing to comply with mandatory hijab rules.

Previously, some media outlets, including Javan, a newspaper affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have described cafes as "gathering places for protesters" who, in their view, pose a threat to "national security."

Most recently, the "Vanak Park" cafes in Tehran were sealed, resulting in at least 200 people losing their jobs.

Crackdown on cafes

Authorities believe cafes, because of their widespread presence and popularity, could play a role in organizing mass protests.

The government's fears are rooted in the latest wave of protests in Iran, which began on December 28, 2025, and grew into the country's largest uprising since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Saediniya, a well-known cafe chain with 10 branches in Iran, closed its branches on this day in support of calls for strikes. It was subsequently accused of engaging in "propaganda against the state."

Iran's Supreme Court has now upheld the sentence of Sadegh Saedinia, the owner of the cafe chain, to 12 years and six months in prison, along with the confiscation of his assets.

He was arrested over his support for the protests, and all branches of his cafe chain were confiscated and shut down by judicial order.

Other cafes, including "Lamiz" and "Voria," faced a broadly similar fate. Voria is owned by a prominent Iranian footballer. Both were sealed by judicial order because of their indirect support for calls to protest. Cafe closures have not been confined to periods of protest, however, and the practice continues.

The rise of the cafe culture

Tehran has seen a surge in the number of cafes over the past decade, rising from around 300 in the early 2010s to as many as 4,000 now, according to various estimates.

Some experts attribute the growing number to changes in urban lifestyles in recent years. They see this as more than the expansion of a particular type of business and describe it as a sign of wider social and cultural changes within Iranian society.

"The explosive growth of cafes in society can, to some extent, be seen as a social response to living in a state of chronic crisis," Saba Alaleh, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst whose work focuses on political and social issues, told DW's Persian service.

"In such circumstances, people are not simply looking to consume or be entertained. They are looking for a place to temporarily distance themselves from the pressures of everyday life," she said.

"In this sense, the cafe becomes a third space. It is neither home nor the workplace, but a space between the two where people can briefly step away from their everyday roles and pressures, connect with others, and feel that life is still somewhat manageable and normal."

The cafe trend has become particularly popular among Gen Z, who are bearing the brunt of runaway inflation and steep living costs in Iran.

"The young people who gather in these cafes do not necessarily come from affluent backgrounds," Nasser, a cafe owner in Tehran, told DW. "In many parts of Tehran, young people from the middle class also meet at cafes, and many of our customers belong to this group."

The political role of cafes

Even before the latest bout of nationwide protests that began at the end of last year, shutting down cafes was common practice for the Iranian government.

Most of these crackdowns and closures, however, were carried out under the pretext of enforcing compulsory hijab.

The protests that began in late December 2025 changed that, with cafes becoming the target more often and for varied reasons.

"They shut down our cafe on the pretext that we had served customers who were not wearing the hijab, but that is only an excuse," Nasser said.

"Outside, on the streets of Tehran, women and girls have effectively abandoned the compulsory hijab, yet the government expects us not to allow them into the cafe," he added.

Maintaining control over social spaces

Alaleh said the issue is no longer simply about cracking down on women for not wearing the hijab.

"Authoritarian governments generally seek to control the flow of information, social interactions and the organization of citizens," she pointed out. "Any space beyond the direct supervision of those in power that allows trust, dialogue and social ties to develop can weaken part of the government's monopoly over the social sphere."

The expert said the crackdown on cafes and cafegoers is part of the government's efforts to preserve its monopoly over social spaces.

She underlined that to a security apparatus, even a group of young people casually sitting together can represent the emergence of an independent social network outside the formal structures of power.

"The broader and more deeply rooted these independent networks become, the more difficult it is for the government to maintain exclusive control over the public sphere," added Alaleh.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Ethiopia's constitutional reform: What does it mean — especially for Abiy?
entries.summary: Does Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed stand to benefit from a planned constitutional reform in the country? A new presidential system would reshape political power — and could give him even more power in office.
entries.content:
Ethiopia

Ethiopia: What does constitutional reform mean for Abiy?

September 9, 2026

Does Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed stand to benefit from a planned constitutional reform in the country? A new presidential system would reshape political power — and could give him even more power in office.

Since 2018, Abiy Ahmedhas been the most powerful man in Ethiopian politics, governing the country during some of its most trying days in recent history. From the Tigray war to a feeble but lasting peace with neighboring Eritrea, Abiy has actively shaped and reshaped Ethiopia's role in Africa and indeed the world.

Soon, he might even get to consolidate more power and influence in his office, as Ethiopia's political system might fundamentally change in the future.

Following weeks-long consultations, there are indications that the offices of prime minister and president could potentially be merged. This would mean that the largely ceremonial presidency could thus become the center of political power in the country.

While details about the precise re-designing of the system remain unclear, local reports say that the consultations indeed resulted in a positive recommendation to create a stronger presidency.

For Abiy, that would likely be a remarkable prospect.

Support for a new office

During a drawn-out national dialogue with around 4,000 delegates in Addis Ababa in recent weeks, participants discussed some of the country's key political conflict, including the overall structure of the state, ongoing ethnic tensions, the rule of law and human rights — as well as the role of the prime minister.

Abiy did not take part in these meetings but could benefit significantly from their endorsement of a presidential system.

One key element for any constitutional reform to be pushed through parliament is already in place: Abiy won June's parliamentary elections with a massive majority, which could help him and his party with advocating for a presidency with broader executive powers. 

Benefits of a stronger presidency

Supporters of a stronger presidency see it as a way of bringing Ethiopia's ethnically and regionally fragmented society closer together.

They say a president representing the country as a whole could help strengthen a national political identity.

Befeqadu Hailu, an Ethiopian civil rights activist and political commentator, told DW that this might be a strength of the proposed new system, and that a president directly elected by the public would have a stronger mandate to govern.

Hailu believes that in future elections, a presidential candidate would have to convince "more than one ethnic group and more than one religious group" to win an election, which could help strengthen democratic processes.

At the same time, he issued a warning that "[p]residential systems are more prone to descending into dictatorship."

How much more power is there to take?

But the key question is not who would become president, but rather what powers this office would have — as well as who would be tasked with holding the president to account.

Ethiopia already has a powerful executive branch and since taking office in 2018, Abiy has consolidated more and more political power.

The creation of the Prosperity Party in 2019 under his leadership out of a number of coalition partners has already considerably reshaped the country's political system, significantly limiting the role of the opposition.

Abiy also controls the military and security apparatus, with little power left to grab under a new system.

For British journalist and Ethiopia expert Martin Plaut, the proposed reform is therefore less of a transfer of power to one person that an act of "formalizing the situation that currently exists."

'Legal does not mean legitimate'

The proposed reform also raises a fundamental question about democratic processes: Can such a concentration of power be viewed as the will of the people if it is enacted through legal procedures in parliament? Or should there perhaps be a plebiscite on the proposed changes?

In this context, civil rights activist Hailu highlights the importance of distinguishing between procedural and popular legitimacy.

In Ethiopia, he says, existing political institutions have "procedural legitimacy" to enact such changes while they lack broad "popular legitimacy."

Hailu says bluntly that "no one believes that Ethiopia has ever had democratic elections," referring to the most recent parliamentary election, which took place under difficult conditions: Voting was not possible in several conflict-ridden regions of the country, while opposition parties reported instances of restrictions and repression.

It is therefore unclear to what extent the result of the poll can be regarded as democratically legitimate — yet it is seen as the official result.

This is why Hailu believes that parliament may have the formal authority to amend the constitution and introduce a presidential system while still being only partially representative of the voting populace.

Who was actually included in the process?

Another issue is not only what was recommended by those participating in the national dialogue but also who exactly took part in it — and who didn't.

The composition of the dialogue, which eventually issued the recommendation to change the current system, is a major concern, as opposition parties boycotted the process, while influencial armed groups with strong political aspirations were equally not represented.

Despite certain valid reservations about some of these movements, the result was that some of the major political forces most directly involved in Ethiopia's current conflicts were absent.

Plaut says this leaves only one conclusion: "Without the opposition parties and armed factions, the process lacks the backing of groups that feel alienated by the current system."

"I'm sure that the Prime Minister will get what he wants," Plaut says, describing the dialogue as merely a "rubber-stamping exercise."

Hailu also shared some critical views on the lack of political inclusion of opposing groups, arguing that it was ultimately aimed at implementing changes "based on the vision of the Prosperity Party itself."

No resolution in sight for Ethiopia's neverending conflicts

Ethiopia's biggest challenges meanwhile are unlikely to be solved with a different style of leadership.

Armed conflicts continue in Oromia and Amhara; the 2020-2022 war in Tigray left deep political and social divisions, with many political and territorial issues remaining unresolved despite promising peace initiatives. And nearly half the population continue to live below the poverty line.

Plaut thinks that a new system of government will hardly address these problems; he believes that the proposed reforms amount to little more than "sticking a band-aid on what is a gaping wound."

The relationship between centralized power in Addis Ababa and Ethiopia's more than 80 ethnic groups remains unresolved, he argues. Previous attempts to ease tensions between the center and the periphery have failed.

In Plaut's view, the underlying tensions between the central government and Ethiopia's various ethnic and regional groups have to be resolved first.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: Oil prices rise as Middle East conflict escalates
entries.summary: The price of oil returned to triple digits in US dollars, as conflict in the Middle East threatens supply chains and puts a strain on global reserves.
entries.content:
September 9, 2026

The price of oil returned to triple digits in US dollars, as conflict in the Middle East threatens supply chains and puts a strain on global reserves.

Oil crude prices topped $100 ($86) a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July amid concerns over oil supplies due to the conflict in the Middle East. 

"The move towards and back above $100 Brent is reflecting a market that increasingly must change its view on how long the Middle East crisis will continue to curb supply from the region," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at the Danish Saxo Bank.

The attacks on Saudi energy facilities by the Iranian-backed Houthisthreaten oil shipments on the Red Sea. This has been a key alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz path. 

Meanwhile, the US attacked Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and in the Strait of Hormuz. "Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies," CENTCOM said in a statement.

Runing out of stock

Since the conflict in the Middle East started, oil exports have been reduced significantly, making some countries turn to their reserves. 

The US has reported its lowest oil reserve since 1982, holding 289.7 million barrels. Former US President Joe Biden and President Donald Trump have used the reserve to cushion consumer prices amid the crisis.

The new price of the barrel is still below the peak reached early this year. In April, Brent jumped to $126 a barrel. Experts believe this is a big risk to a market with little room for capacity to absorb new disruptions occasioned by the war.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

Syria

Syria arms depot explosion kills at least 14

September 9, 2026

The explosion struck near the Syrian city of Sarmada in Idlib province in the northwest. The Defense Ministry said the weapons and remnants from the war were being stored temporarily at the site before being relocated.

Syrian authorities reported that at least 14 people were killed and another 11 wounded on Wednesday as a result of an explosion at a temporary site used to store weapons and remnants of the country's long-running civil war. 

The explosion took place near the city of Sarmada in the northwestern Idlib province.

What do we know about the explosion?

Syria's Defense Ministry said the weapons and war remnants were being stored termporarily at the site before being transported elsewhere. It said that some of its personnel were among those wounded.

The explosion in an area full of volatile materials led to secondary explosions and fires that hampered the emergency response. Smoke billowed from the blast site for some time on Wednesday.

"The toll from the explosion in a temporary storage for collecting weapons and war remnants near the city of Sarmada ... registered 14 killed and 11 injured in a preliminary count," the Idlib health department said.

Authorities have not yet said what caused the explosion.

It was the second fatal incident of its kind in Idlib province this month. On September 1, five people were killed and others were wounded when a vehicle carrying ammunition exploded in Binnish.

Syria only recently emerged from more than a decade of civil war, when forces loyal to new President Ahmed al-Sharaa ousted Bashar Assad and took control of Damascus. Idlib was one of the hardest-hit regions in the country during the war.
